title: Mike Mentzer: Mustachioed fraud or Bodybuilding genius? (THE HIT
summary: After watching hours of Mentzer lectures, NH lays out HIT (one set to failure per exercise, about 4 sets per session, 96 hours between sessions) fairly and then critiques it. He argues set multiplication lets you train both hard and long, that intensity caps at 100% while volume and frequency can still rise, that 'more rest' is a bad plateau fix, and that Mentzer's rigid, fear-based dogma should be dropped while keeping his emphasis on hard sets.
claims: NH's earlier Mentzer video was poorly researched and biased; this one is based on hours of his lectures
Mentzer's physique can't validate HIT because he used PEDs, and everything works for PED users and for beginners
HIT appeared in the high-volume era, when Arnold trained three to four hours a day, sometimes twice a day
Mentzer's core premise: you can train hard or long but not both; growth comes from intense work, so training should be high intensity, low volume, low frequency
A Mentzer chest and back day: one set of 6-10 pec deck supersetted with 1-3 reps of incline press, one set of 6-10 pulldowns, then 5-8 deadlifts, four sets to failure in total
Mentzer prescribed about 96 hours of rest between sessions, i.e. training once every four days, and called anything more overtraining
Mentzer believed a muscle's adaptive threshold is very low and any extra set wastes or interferes with recovery
Set multiplication defeats the hard-or-long logic: split a 30-rep squat set into three and every rep is intense, with more total work
It is dubious that one or two extra sets could completely stop progress
Intensity is capped at 100% while volume and frequency can keep increasing, so an intensity-only program runs out of room
Mentzer's plateau fix of adding rest days until training once every five days makes people regress if their real problem is too little stimulus
Forced reps and beyond-failure techniques are mostly an extra set disguised; why not rest and do a fresh set
Mentzer's claim that EZ curl bars don't work the biceps is unjustified guru talk
Good programming advice is good regardless of who says it; HIT is carried by Mentzer's charisma
Mentzer advised taking two to three weeks completely off before starting HIT to recover from overtraining
Intensity accumulates: four sets at 90% beat one set at 100% overall
A muscle does not need a full week to recover from damage, so trading frequency for intensity is questionable
A beyond-failure set that is so fatiguing has a poor stimulus-to-fatigue ratio
Sets taken at 70-90% intensity also grow muscle; failure is not the only way
Mentzer used fear: everything you did before was wasted, don't change exercise order or selection
Lifters obsess over exact set numbers out of fear of being one or two sets off; the body is not that fragile
NH's programming is holistic: volume, intensity and frequency form a trinity that influence each other
Keep Mentzer's understanding of hard sets, but to keep working harder you eventually must train longer and more often
exercises: one set 6-10 to failure, superset with incline press
Mentzer claimed it doesn't work biceps; NH rejects this
